title: FAST vs GIKI vs COMSATS for Computer Science: Which to Prioritize
excerpt: Three different merit formulas, three different tests, three different kinds of student rewarded. Here's how FAST, GIKI, and COMSATS actually compare for CS, and how to decide where your prep time goes.

content.text: Three respected names, three very different formulas

If Computer Science is your goal, FAST, GIKI, and COMSATS are three of the most commonly considered options — and students often compare them on reputation alone, without realizing their merit formulas reward genuinely different student profiles. Knowing the actual numbers before you decide where to focus is worth more than going on name recognition.
The core difference comes down to how much each university weighs your entry test against your FSc percentage:

items: GIKI: 15% (Matric or last completed qualification) + 85% Admission Test — FSc/Intermediate marks aren't included at all, only used as an eligibility threshold
COMSATS: 10% Matric + 40% FSc + 50% NTS-NAT (or COMSATS's own accepted test)

content.text: These formulas are set independently by each university and can be revised between admission cycles — confirm current figures at nu.edu.pk, giki.edu.pk, and comsats.edu.pk before building a prep plan around them, especially since GIKI's formula in particular has no FSc component to fall back on.
Why GIKI is the outlier of the three

The most important thing to understand about GIKI is that your FSc or A-Level percentage isn't part of the merit calculation at all beyond meeting a minimum eligibility threshold (typically around 60%). Once you clear that bar, your entire aggregate comes down to your Matric percentage (15%) and your GIKI Admission Test score (85%) — an even more test-dominant formula than NUST's.

This makes GIKI the university where a strong FSc record does you the least good in the numbers, and where entry test performance does almost all the work. If your FSc percentage is average but you test exceptionally well under timed pressure, GIKI's formula rewards that profile more than either FAST's or COMSATS's.
FAST and COMSATS: similar formulas, different tests

FAST and COMSATS actually use nearly identical weightings — both are 10% Matric, 40% FSc, 50% entry test. That means, on paper, these two universities reward the same kind of student profile: someone with a solid, consistent FSc record who also performs reasonably well on the entry test, since neither factor can fully compensate for serious weakness in the other.

Where they differ is the test itself. FAST uses its own NU Entry Test (Advanced Math, Basic Math, English, and Analytical/IQ Reasoning), while COMSATS generally requires an NTS NAT score rather than running its own separate test. If you're already NTS-familiar or have taken NAT for other applications, that score can carry directly into a COMSATS aggregate without sitting an additional exam — a genuine time-saver if you're juggling multiple applications.
What this means for where you put your prep hours

items: If your FSc record is strong and consistent: FAST and COMSATS's formulas reward that directly, since FSc carries a real 40% share in both. GIKI's formula won't give you the same credit for it.
If you test exceptionally well under time pressure but your FSc record is average: GIKI's 85% test-weighting gives you the most room to make up ground through the test alone.

If you're already preparing for NTS NAT for other universities: that same prep transfers directly to a COMSATS application without additional test-specific prep, since COMSATS doesn't require its own separate entry test.

content.text: The tests themselves aren't interchangeable either

Beyond the formulas, the actual exams differ in content and structure. FAST's test is Math-heavy across two difficulty tiers, plus English and a distinct Analytical/IQ Reasoning section. GIKI's Admission Test covers Mathematics, Physics, and English only — no IQ/reasoning component, and no Chemistry either, since it's built for engineering and computing programs broadly. COMSATS applicants generally sit the NTS NAT, which has its own separate structure and syllabus distinct from either university's own test.

This means prep genuinely diverges once you look past "it's all Math and reasoning" — a student who's built strong FAST-style IQ reasoning skills isn't necessarily well-prepared for GIKI's Physics-heavy paper, and vice versa.
Applying to more than one isn't a bad idea

Since these are three separate applications with three separate formulas and tests, applying to more than one where you're eligible is a reasonable way to hedge rather than something to avoid. The overlap in core Mathematics preparation carries across all three to some extent, but treating each one's specific format and formula as genuinely distinct — rather than assuming "CS prep is CS prep" — is what actually protects your chances across all three.

If you have to prioritize because of limited time, the more useful question isn't which university is more prestigious, but which formula rewards the profile you actually have right now — your real FSc trajectory and your demonstrated test performance under timed conditions — rather than deciding this in the abstract before you've run your own numbers through each one.

items.question: What is the main difference between FAST, GIKI, and COMSATS merit formulas?
items.answer: FAST and COMSATS both weigh merit as 10% Matric + 40% FSc + 50% entry test. GIKI is the outlier — 15% Matric (or last completed qualification) + 85% Admission Test, with FSc used only as a minimum eligibility threshold, not counted in the aggregate itself.

items.question: Does GIKI count your FSc percentage toward merit?
items.answer: No — beyond clearing a minimum eligibility threshold (typically around 60%), your FSc percentage isn't part of GIKI's merit calculation at all. Your aggregate comes down almost entirely to your Matric percentage and Admission Test score.

items.question: Do FAST and COMSATS use the same entry test?
items.answer: No. FAST runs its own NU Entry Test (Advanced Math, Basic Math, English, and Analytical/IQ Reasoning). COMSATS generally requires an NTS NAT score instead of a university-run test, so NAT prep done for other applications can carry directly into a COMSATS application.

items.question: Which university's formula rewards a strong FSc record the most?
items.answer: FAST and COMSATS both give FSc a real 40% share of the aggregate, so a strong, consistent FSc record is rewarded directly at either. GIKI's formula gives no credit for FSc beyond the eligibility threshold, so it rewards test performance far more than academic record.

items.question: Should I apply to all three universities?
items.answer: Applying to more than one where you're eligible is a reasonable hedge, since each is a separate application with its own formula and test. Core Mathematics prep overlaps across all three to some extent, but each test's specific format still needs its own dedicated preparation.
